topics.label: Lecture opening and overview of cellular transformation and cancer genetics
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic frames the lecture, connects it to the practicals, and previews its learning outcomes rather than developing a substantive subject.

topics.label: Tumor virology and the cellular origins of oncogenes
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how the discovery of tumor-causing viruses led to the recognition that transforming viral genes originate from cellular proto-oncogenes.

topics.label: Experimental assays of cellular transformation
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic describes laboratory assays used to test whether genes or mutations confer transformed properties on cells.

topics.label: Functional classifications of cancer genes and mutations
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic introduces the classifications used to describe how cancer-associated mutations affect tumor formation and cellular functions.

topics.label: Mutation effects in cell-cycle control genes
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show how mutations affecting RB and p53 alter cell-cycle control, including how the specific mutation can determine its functional effect.

topics.label: Genetic instability from repair, replication, and mitotic failures
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how failures in genome maintenance and cell division generate genetic instability and affect tumor cells.

topics.label: Timing of mutations in colorectal cancer progression
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic considers when mutations arise during colorectal tumor development and how their order affects progression.

topics.label: Hereditary cancer predisposition
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how inherited mutations confer cancer risk and illustrates that risk through caretaker and gatekeeper genes and hereditary syndromes.

topics.label: BRCA2 restoration and whether genetic instability is required for malignancy
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic uses BRCA2 restoration during treatment to show that a tumor can remain malignant after its instability-associated repair defect is reversed.

topics.label: Lecture close, further reading, and next lecture
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic closes the lecture, invites questions, recommends reading, and previews the next lecture.
